opus-5.5.text:
I think what Kimi Linear did well is that they didn't treat hardware efficiency as an afterthought. A lot of linear attention papers propose a nice recurrence on paper, and then you discover it doesn't map well onto GPUs. You end up with something that's theoretically linear-time but slower than FlashAttention in practice. That gap has been the field's real problem for years.

Their core module, Kimi Delta Attention, builds on the gated delta rule line of work. The key change is moving from a scalar, head-wise forget gate to a finer-grained, channel-wise gate. That gives the model more expressive control over what it forgets. But as soon as you make the gate fine-grained, you risk losing the structure that makes chunkwise parallel training efficient. In the general diagonal-plus-low-rank formulation you get numerical stability issues and a lot of extra computation, because you have to handle those decays inside the chunk carefully, often in log space or with secondary chunking.

What I appreciate is that they made a deliberate trade-off. They constrained the parameterization so the transition matrix keeps a specific structure. That lets the chunkwise algorithm reuse computation and run mostly as matrix multiplications on tensor cores, instead of falling back to elementwise or sequential operations. That's really the whole game. On modern GPUs, if your work isn't expressed as matmuls, you're leaving most of the hardware's throughput on the table. So they gave up a bit of generality relative to a fully general DPLR form and got a much more efficient kernel in return. I think that's the right engineering instinct.

The second thing is the hybrid design. They interleave KDA layers with a smaller number of full attention layers, roughly three linear layers for every global attention layer. From a systems perspective, that's pragmatic. Most of the KV cache and decoding cost goes away, which matters a lot for long-context inference and for things like RL rollouts, where you generate very long sequences. You still keep some global attention for the retrieval-heavy behavior where pure linear models are weaker. People sometimes see hybrids as a compromise, but I see them as where the field has converged for good reason. The linear layers handle state tracking and local compression cheaply, and the attention layers handle precise recall.

Also, they built on and contributed to open kernel infrastructure, so other people can actually use and verify this. In this area, an architecture is only as good as its kernel. If the community can't run it efficiently, it won't get adopted.

If I had a caveat, it's that the remaining bottlenecks are less about FLOPs and more about memory movement and how well these kernels do at different sequence lengths and batch sizes, especially in inference serving systems built around attention and paged KV caches. Getting linear-attention state management into those serving stacks is still ongoing work. But overall, I'd say Kimi Linear is one of the clearest examples of co-designing the algorithm and the hardware together, and showing that it can hold up at real scale rather than just in small experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Kimi Linear is a good example of what happens when you design an architecture with the hardware in mind from day one, rather than inventing something mathematically elegant and then hoping the kernel engineers can rescue it later.

The core idea in Kimi Delta Attention is to take the gated delta rule and make the gating channel-wise instead of scalar. On paper that's a modest change. In practice it is painful, because the delta rule already requires you to compute things like products of Householder-style transforms inside a chunk, and once the decay becomes a per-channel diagonal you lose some of the nice algebraic shortcuts that made chunkwise parallelism cheap. So the interesting part of their work, to me, is not the equation itself but the fact that they worked out a chunkwise formulation that keeps the matrix multiplications dense and tensor-core friendly. They use a specialized variant of the DPLR representation, and they are careful to avoid the parts of general DPLR that blow up in cost. You end up with something that is more expressive than Mamba2-style scalar decay, but with a kernel that is not that much slower than GDN in practice. That trade-off is very deliberate.

The second thing I'd point to is the hybrid ratio. They settled on roughly three linear layers to one full attention layer, and the full attention layers have no positional encoding. That's a hardware decision as much as a modeling one. The linear layers keep the KV cache small and the decoding memory traffic low, and the global layers give you the retrieval capability that pure linear models still struggle with. Pushing the ratio further toward linear saves more memory but you start paying in long-context quality, so 3:1 is a pragmatic point on the Pareto curve rather than some magic number.

Where I'd be a bit cautious is in reading the speedups too literally. The headline numbers show up mostly at very long context, like a million tokens, where the KV cache of a standard transformer is the dominant cost. At shorter sequence lengths the gap is much narrower, and the quality of your kernel implementation matters more than the architecture. They did invest in that, and the fact that they open-sourced kernels into fla means other people can actually reproduce the efficiency rather than take it on faith, which I think is the right way to do this.

So overall I'd say the hardware thinking is sound. It's not that they discovered a new primitive, it's that they made a series of disciplined choices, fine-grained gating, chunkwise dense matmuls, a sensible hybrid ratio, and validated them at a scale where the choices actually matter. That's harder than it sounds.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the architectural idea from the hardware results. An architecture can reduce the amount of computation on paper, but the practical benefit depends on how well its operations map onto the hardware—memory access, parallelism, and kernel efficiency all matter.

I don’t have enough detail here to judge Kimi Linear’s specific implementation. What I’d want to see is end-to-end performance at comparable model quality, across different context lengths and batch sizes. If the gains hold across those settings, that would be stronger evidence of effective hardware optimization than a single headline benchmark.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d judge it by whether the algorithm translates into real efficiency on the hardware. Reducing the theoretical computation is only part of the story—you also have to consider memory traffic, parallelism, and how much overhead the implementation introduces.

For Kimi Linear, I’d want to see end-to-end measurements: latency, throughput, and memory use at comparable model quality, across different sequence lengths and batch sizes. Without those details here, I wouldn’t make a strong claim about its hardware optimization. The important question is whether the gains hold up under realistic workloads.
